claim: Cell bodies of iPNs are exclusively located in the ventral cell cluster which consists of ∼50 iPNs.
source: Cell bodies of iPNs are exclusively located in the ventral cell cluster which consists of ∼50 iPNs (Lai et al., 2008) that project via the mACT to the LH, thereby bypassing the MBc (Ito et al., 1997) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lai et al., 2008 and Ito et al., 1997, and reference to Figure 1A,B

claim: iPNs project via the mACT to the LH, thereby bypassing the MBc.
source: Cell bodies of iPNs are exclusively located in the ventral cell cluster which consists of ∼50 iPNs (Lai et al., 2008) that project via the mACT to the LH, thereby bypassing the MBc (Ito et al., 1997) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito et al., 1997 and reference to Figure 1A,B

claim: ePN somata are located anterodorsally and laterally of the AL.
source: In contrast, ePN somata are located anterodorsally and laterally of the AL, and their axons project through the iACT or oACT to the MBc and the LH (Stocker et al., 1997; Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stocker et al., 1997; Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2008

claim: ePN axons project through the iACT or oACT to the MBc and the LH.
source: In contrast, ePN somata are located anterodorsally and laterally of the AL, and their axons project through the iACT or oACT to the MBc and the LH (Stocker et al., 1997; Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stocker et al., 1997; Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2008

claim: Both PN types innervate overlapping regions in the AL and the LH.
source: Double-labeling shows that both PN types innervate overlapping regions in the AL and the LH, while a small posterior-lateral LH area is targeted only by ePNs (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A small posterior-lateral LH area is targeted only by ePNs.
source: Double-labeling shows that both PN types innervate overlapping regions in the AL and the LH, while a small posterior-lateral LH area is targeted only by ePNs (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In GH146-positive PNs, immunolabeling reveals GABA production in all ∼6 PNs of the ventral cell cluster.
source: In GH146-positive (GH146+) PNs, immunolabeling reveals GABA production in all ∼6 PNs of the ventral cell cluster (Wilson and Laurent, 2005), whereas ePNs of this line are exclusively cholinergic (Shang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wilson and Laurent, 2005 and Shang et al., 2007

claim: ePNs of the GH146 line are exclusively cholinergic.
source: In GH146-positive (GH146+) PNs, immunolabeling reveals GABA production in all ∼6 PNs of the ventral cell cluster (Wilson and Laurent, 2005), whereas ePNs of this line are exclusively cholinergic (Shang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shang et al., 2007

claim: For the ∼45 MZ699-positive iPNs, GAD1 in situ hybridizations imply GABA synthesis.
source: For the ∼45 MZ699-positive (MZ699+) iPNs (Lai et al., 2008), GAD1 (glutamic acid decarboxylase) in situ hybridizations imply GABA synthesis (Okada et al., 2009), which was recently verified via immunostaining (Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lai et al., 2008; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013

claim: GABA synthesis in MZ699+ iPNs was recently verified via immunostaining.
source: For the ∼45 MZ699-positive (MZ699+) iPNs (Lai et al., 2008), GAD1 (glutamic acid decarboxylase) in situ hybridizations imply GABA synthesis (Okada et al., 2009), which was recently verified via immunostaining (Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013

claim: Both PN populations possess dendritic regions in the AL, indicating the AL as their cholinergic input site.
source: The polarity of both PN populations has been studied in detail, showing that both possess dendritic regions in the AL, indicating the AL as their cholinergic input site, while the LH represents their major output site (Jefferis et al., 2001; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jefferis et al., 2001; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013

claim: The LH represents the major output site for both PN populations.
source: The polarity of both PN populations has been studied in detail, showing that both possess dendritic regions in the AL, indicating the AL as their cholinergic input site, while the LH represents their major output site (Jefferis et al., 2001; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jefferis et al., 2001; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013

claim: 75% of AL glomeruli were innervated by MZ699+ iPNs (40 out of 53 glomeruli).
source: The reconstruction and identification of all AL glomeruli provided 53 glomeruli, of which 75% were innervated by MZ699+ iPNs (40) while 70% (37) were covered by GH146+ ePNs (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: 70% of AL glomeruli were covered by GH146+ ePNs (37 out of 53 glomeruli).
source: The reconstruction and identification of all AL glomeruli provided 53 glomeruli, of which 75% were innervated by MZ699+ iPNs (40) while 70% (37) were covered by GH146+ ePNs (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: 55% of all glomeruli were innervated by both MZ699 and GH146 lines.
source: 55% of all glomeruli were innervated by both lines.
evidence: Stated as a direct observation from the data

claim: Dendritic MZ699-GAL4 innervation density was not homogeneous across glomeruli.
source: Notably, dendritic MZ699-GAL4 innervation density was not homogeneous. Certain glomeruli were densely innervated (e.g., DM2, DM4 and DM5), while others did not reveal any postsynaptic sites (e.g., DL1, DL4 and DL5).
evidence: Supported by specific examples of glomeruli with different innervation patterns

claim: MZ699+ iPNs target specific glomerular subsets selectively, suggesting these neurons have a particular function within the olfactory network.
source: Hence MZ699+ iPNs target specific glomerular subsets selectively, which suggests that these neurons have a particular function within the olfactory network.
evidence: Inference drawn from the selective innervation pattern observed

claim: Odor evoked Ca2+ responses separate in certain regions of the LH in an odor-specific and concentration-dependent manner.
source: We observed that odor evoked Ca2+ responses separate in certain regions of the LH in an odor-specific and concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2C showing imaging data

claim: Acetoin acetate and balsamic vinegar evoked Ca2+ activity in spatially similar regions.
source: Acetoin acetate and balsamic vinegar evoked Ca2+ activity in spatially similar regions.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging experiments

claim: At higher concentrations, an additional region was recruited for acetoin acetate and balsamic vinegar.
source: At higher concentrations, an additional region was recruited.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging experiments

claim: Benzaldehyde elicited no response at very low concentrations, but induced clear activity at median and high concentrations in a third region, which was completely separate from the regions activated by the other two odors.
source: Benzaldehyde elicited no response at very low concentrations, but induced clear activity at median and high concentrations in a third region, which was completely separate from the regions activated by the other two odors.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging experiments

claim: Observed patterns were highly reproducible within one animal and stereotypic among different individuals.
source: Observed patterns were highly reproducible within one animal and stereotypic among different individuals, as shown for the stimulation with 1-octen-3-ol (Figure 2D) as well as other odors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: NNMF analysis extracted three clearly reproducible and spatially robust LH odor response domains (ORDs).
source: The NNMF analysis extracted three clearly reproducible and spatially robust ORDs (Figure 2E, see NNMF part in the 'Materials and methods' section).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2E and methods description

claim: ORDs occupying common temporal kinetics exhibited highly stereotypic spatial patterns.
source: Notably, ORDs occupying common temporal kinetics exhibited highly stereotypic spatial patterns.
evidence: Direct observation from NNMF analysis

claim: The three ORDs were termed LH-PM (LH-posterior-medial), LH-AM (LH-anterior-medial) and LH-AL (LH-anterior-lateral) according to their anatomical positions.
source: We termed the ORDs LH-PM (LH-posterior-medial), LH-AM (LH-anterior-medial) and LH-AL (LH-anterior-lateral) according to their anatomical positions.
evidence: Nomenclature defined based on anatomical location

claim: Analysis of additional odorants revealed neuronal activity exclusively within the three described ORDs.
source: Remarkably, analysis of the additional odorants revealed neuronal activity exclusively within the three described ORDs (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplements 2,3).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2F and supplementary figures

claim: The LH-PM area chiefly revealed robust odor-evoked responses across concentrations.
source: The LH-PM area chiefly revealed robust odor-evoked responses across concentrations, while the LH-AM and LH-AL were mainly activated at very high odor concentrations by distinct odorants.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data

claim: The LH-AM and LH-AL were mainly activated at very high odor concentrations by distinct odorants.
source: The LH-PM area chiefly revealed robust odor-evoked responses across concentrations, while the LH-AM and LH-AL were mainly activated at very high odor concentrations by distinct odorants.
evidence: Direct observation from imaging data

claim: MZ699+ iPNs could be assigned to two major morphological classes based on their innervation pattern in the LH.
source: Based on their innervation pattern in the LH, MZ699+ iPNs could be assigned to two major morphological classes (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3B,C showing neuronal reconstructions

claim: One iPN group diverged to the LH-PM region (8/25 of iPNs).
source: As expected from the extracted ORDs, one iPN group diverged to the LH-PM region (8/25 of iPNs), while a second group extended their axonal terminations within the LH-AM area (10/25 of iPNs).
evidence: Direct count from neuronal tracing experiments

claim: A second iPN group extended their axonal terminations within the LH-AM area (10/25 of iPNs).
source: As expected from the extracted ORDs, one iPN group diverged to the LH-PM region (8/25 of iPNs), while a second group extended their axonal terminations within the LH-AM area (10/25 of iPNs).
evidence: Direct count from neuronal tracing experiments

claim: All except one iPN could be clustered according to their target region in either the LH-AM or LH-PM area.
source: The dendrogram of morphological similarity between each individual iPN shows that all, except one iPN, could be clustered according to their target region in either the LH-AM or LH-PM area (Figure 3D) which confirms the classification into two major categories.
evidence: Supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Both neuronal classes possess significantly different target areas in the LH (p < 0.001).
source: Additionally, we performed a principal component analysis based on the distances of the similarity scores showing that both neuronal classes possess significantly different target areas in the LH (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; p < 0.001, one-way ANOSIM).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: MZ699+ iPNs develop mainly oligoglomerular patterns innervating on average 5.4 ± 3.9 glomeruli.
source: Instead, MZ699+ iPNs develop mainly oligoglomerular patterns innervating on average 5.4 ± 3.9 glomeruli (mean ± SD), which are not necessarily in close proximity.
evidence: Direct measurement from neuronal tracing data

claim: LH-PM iPNs extended dendrites mainly into glomeruli from the ventro- or dorsomedial area of the AL (e.g., DM4, DM2, VM7, VM5d).
source: Whereas LH-PM iPNs extended dendrites mainly into glomeruli from the ventro- or dorsomedial area of the AL (e.g., DM4, DM2, VM7, VM5d), iPNs targeting the LH-AM zone innervated glomeruli ranging from the ventro- and dorsoanterior to the dorsocentral region (e.g., DC3, VC1, VA6, VL1).
evidence: Direct observation from neuronal tracing data

claim: iPNs targeting the LH-AM zone innervated glomeruli ranging from the ventro- and dorsoanterior to the dorsocentral region (e.g., DC3, VC1, VA6, VL1).
source: Whereas LH-PM iPNs extended dendrites mainly into glomeruli from the ventro- or dorsomedial area of the AL (e.g., DM4, DM2, VM7, VM5d), iPNs targeting the LH-AM zone innervated glomeruli ranging from the ventro- and dorsoanterior to the dorsocentral region (e.g., DC3, VC1, VA6, VL1).
evidence: Direct observation from neuronal tracing data

claim: iPNs targeting the LH-PM region innervate a significantly different glomerular subset than iPNs that send their axonal terminals to the LH-AM area (p < 0.001).
source: This finding is further supported by a principal component analysis showing that iPNs targeting the LH-PM region innervate a significant different glomerular subset than iPNs that send their axonal terminals to the LH-AM area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; p < 0.001, one-way ANOSIM).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: A few uniglomerular MZ699+ iPNs innervating either glomerulus DA1 or VL1 (4/25 of iPNs) target the LH-AM region.
source: In addition to the oligoglomerular iPNs, we observed a few uniglomerular MZ699+ iPNs innervating either glomerulus DA1 or VL1 (4/25 of iPNs), consistent with Lai et al. (2008), which target the LH-AM region (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct observation from neuronal tracing, consistent with citation to Lai et al., 2008

claim: Three MZ699+ neurons did not innervate the AL and sent their axons through the mACT to the LH and/or the MBc.
source: Moreover, we identified three other MZ699+ neurons that did not innervate the AL and sent their axons through the mACT to the LH and/or the MBc.
evidence: Direct observation from neuronal tracing

claim: Transecting the mACT significantly reduced responses in the LH-PM and LH-AM region.
source: Transecting the mACT significantly reduced responses in the LH-PM and LH-AM region, whereas LH-AL responses were significantly abolished by plF-ablation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by transection experiment data shown in Figure 4D

claim: LH-AL responses were significantly abolished by plF-ablation.
source: Transecting the mACT significantly reduced responses in the LH-PM and LH-AM region, whereas LH-AL responses were significantly abolished by plF-ablation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by transection experiment data shown in Figure 4D

claim: LH-AL responses to some odors were significantly increased after mACT transection as a consequence of the suppression of iPN inhibition of vlPr neurons.
source: Notably, we observed that LH-AL responses to some odors were significantly increased after mACT transection as a consequence of the suppression of iPN inhibition of vlPr neurons confirming the study by Liang et al. (2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Liang et al., 2013

claim: Activity in the LH-PM and LH-AM domain can be assigned to MZ699+ iPNs.
source: Hence, activity in the LH-PM and LH-AM domain can be assigned to MZ699+ iPNs, while LH-AL activity is mainly evoked by vlPr neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inference from transection experiments shown in Figure 4E

claim: LH-AL activity is mainly evoked by vlPr neurons.
source: Hence, activity in the LH-PM and LH-AM domain can be assigned to MZ699+ iPNs, while LH-AL activity is mainly evoked by vlPr neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inference from transection experiments shown in Figure 4E

claim: Flies with silenced MZ699+ iPN GABA production revealed a neutral or aversive behavioral response to attractive odors.
source: Notably, flies with silenced MZ699+ iPN GABA production revealed a neutral or aversive behavioral response to attractive odors, while repellent odors evoked an even stronger aversion (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Repellent odors evoked an even stronger aversion in flies with silenced MZ699+ iPN GABA production.
source: Notably, flies with silenced MZ699+ iPN GABA production revealed a neutral or aversive behavioral response to attractive odors, while repellent odors evoked an even stronger aversion (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C

claim: All responses changed in a negative direction, indicating MZ699+ iPNs play a crucial role in mediating attraction behavior.
source: Indeed, all responses changed in a negative direction, indicating MZ699+ iPNs play a crucial role in mediating attraction behavior.
evidence: Inference from behavioral data analysis

claim: MZ699+ iPNs play a crucial function in mediating attraction behavior by releasing GABA in the LH.
source: Overall, these experiments reveal a crucial function of MZ699+ iPNs in mediating attraction behavior by releasing GABA in the LH.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from behavioral experiments

claim: Attractive and aversive odor representations form separate clusters in the three-dimensional ORD space.
source: When we plotted median odor-evoked activity in a three-dimensional space defined by the three ORDs, we saw a clear clustering of responses evoked by aversive and attractive odorants (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by data visualization shown in Figure 6B

claim: The LH-AL domain, constituted mainly by vlPr neurons, is coding aversive odors.
source: The LH-AL domain, constituted mainly by vlPr neurons, is coding aversive odors, while attractive odors activated only the LH-PM and LH-AM domains that derive from MZ699+ iPNs.
evidence: Inference from correlation of imaging data with behavioral data

claim: Attractive odors activated only the LH-PM and LH-AM domains that derive from MZ699+ iPNs.
source: The LH-AL domain, constituted mainly by vlPr neurons, is coding aversive odors, while attractive odors activated only the LH-PM and LH-AM domains that derive from MZ699+ iPNs.
evidence: Inference from correlation of imaging data with behavioral data

claim: There is a significant correlation between positive valence and the LH-PM domain.
source: As expected, the analysis revealed a significant correlation between positive valence and the LH-PM domain, whereas Ca2+ responses in the LH-AL were strongly negatively correlated to hedonic valence.
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis

claim: Ca2+ responses in the LH-AL were strongly negatively correlated to hedonic valence.
source: As expected, the analysis revealed a significant correlation between positive valence and the LH-PM domain, whereas Ca2+ responses in the LH-AL were strongly negatively correlated to hedonic valence.
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis

claim: The LH-AM domain exhibited a positive but not significant correlation for odor valence.
source: The LH-AM domain exhibited a positive but not significant correlation for odor valence.
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis

claim: Activity within the LH-PM was totally independent of concentration.
source: Remarkably, activity within the LH-PM was totally independent of concentration, whereas activity in both anterior domains was significantly correlated to odor intensity (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: Activity in both anterior domains (LH-AM and LH-AL) was significantly correlated to odor intensity.
source: Remarkably, activity within the LH-PM was totally independent of concentration, whereas activity in both anterior domains was significantly correlated to odor intensity (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: MZ699+ iPNs integrate odor attraction information into the LH-PM domain independent of odor intensity.
source: Hence, MZ699+ iPNs integrate odor attraction information into the LH-PM domain independent of odor intensity, confirming behavioral experiments.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis and behavioral data

claim: Intensity coding is conducted separately by distinct iPNs within the LH-AM domain.
source: Intensity coding is in turn conducted separately by distinct iPNs within the LH-AM domain.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis

claim: Putative third-order vlPr neurons projecting into the LH-AL area code both negative valence and odor intensity.
source: In contrast, putative third-order vlPr neurons projecting into the LH-AL area code both negative valence and odor intensity.
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis

claim: Odor representations in the LH clearly clustered within three separated parts of the correlation matrix, reflecting the observed ORDs.
source: As expected, odor representations in the LH clearly clustered within three separated parts of the matrix, reflecting our observed ORDs.
evidence: Supported by correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: LH coding similarity could not predict AL activity patterns.
source: However, this coding similarity could not predict AL activity patterns, even if the correlation matrix was sorted with respect to pattern similarity in the AL (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by correlation matrix comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3

claim: Most MZ699+ iPNs possess oligoglomerular innervations suggesting that these neurons might not convey precise odor-identity information.
source: Whereas GH146+ ePNs are uniglomerular and retain the topographic code in their axonal arrangement (Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Jefferis et al., 2007), most MZ699+ iPNs possess oligoglomerular innervations suggesting that these neurons might not convey precise odor-identity information.
evidence: Inference from morphological observations and citations to Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Jefferis et al., 2007

claim: MZ699+ iPNs in the AL diverge only into specific glomerular subsets, and so might be pre-determined to selectively extract common features of distinct odors.
source: In addition, MZ699+ iPNs in the AL diverge only into specific glomerular subsets, and so might be pre-determined to selectively extract common features of distinct odors.
evidence: Inference from morphological observations

claim: The AL map at the PN level exhibits a spatial segregation of valence representation.
source: We have previously shown that the AL map at the PN level exhibits a spatial segregation of valence representation (Knaden et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knaden et al., 2012

claim: Certain glomeruli classified as aversion coding at the GH146+ ePN level are omitted by MZ699+ iPNs.
source: Certain glomeruli, which have been classified as aversion coding at the GH146+ ePN level, are omitted by MZ699+ iPNs, whereas most glomeruli classified as attraction coding are particularly densely innervated.
evidence: Direct observation from innervation pattern analysis

claim: Most glomeruli classified as attraction coding are particularly densely innervated by MZ699+ iPNs.
source: Certain glomeruli, which have been classified as aversion coding at the GH146+ ePN level, are omitted by MZ699+ iPNs, whereas most glomeruli classified as attraction coding are particularly densely innervated.
evidence: Direct observation from innervation pattern analysis

claim: Within the MZ699+ iPN population, mainly positive odor traits are extracted, whereas the odor information of negative valence is neglected.
source: These results suggest that within the MZ699+ iPN population, mainly positive odor traits are extracted, whereas the odor information of negative valence is neglected.
evidence: Inference from innervation pattern and functional data

claim: One type of LH neurons receives input from PNs that mainly innervate glomeruli coding fruity-smelling acetates.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the recent finding that one type of LH neurons is receiving input from PNs that mainly innervate glomeruli coding fruity-smelling acetates (Fisek and Wilson, 2014) which represent attractive odor cues (Knaden et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fisek and Wilson, 2014 and Knaden et al., 2012

claim: The MZ699+ iPN population is split into two major morphological classes possessing a clear spatial segregation in the AL which is strictly maintained within the LH.
source: We furthermore demonstrate that the MZ699+ iPN population is split into two major morphological classes possessing a clear spatial segregation in the AL which is strictly maintained within the LH.
evidence: Supported by morphological tracing and cluster analysis

claim: Sensory stimuli of opposing valence are represented in spatially distinct areas within the LH.
source: A recent study that traced the projection pattern of PNs coding ammonia and amines as attractive stimuli and carbon dioxide and acids as repulsive signals suggests that sensory stimuli of opposing valence are represented in spatially distinct areas within the LH (Min et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Min et al., 2013

claim: MZ699+ iPNs selectively suppress the activity of vlPr neurons to food odors, while pheromone responses were not affected.
source: In addition the study by Liang et al. (2013) showed that MZ699+ iPNs selectively suppress the activity of vlPr neurons to food odors, while pheromone responses were not affected verifying the assumption that different odor features are processed separately.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2013

claim: Silencing MB function revealed that the LH alone is sufficient for basic olfactory behavior.
source: Silencing MB function revealed that the LH alone is sufficient for basic olfactory behavior (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Connolly et al., 1996; Heimbeck et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Connolly et al., 1996; Heimbeck et al., 2001

claim: Selectively silencing MZ699+ iPNs severely reduced the flies' odor attraction behavior.
source: Our behavioral results demonstrate that selectively silencing MZ699+ iPNs severely reduced the flies' odor attraction behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data

claim: MZ699+ iPNs are capable of extracting specific features from the combinatorial code emerging in the AL.
source: Hence our results suggest that MZ699+ iPNs are capable of extracting specific features from the combinatorial code emerging in the AL.
evidence: Inference from behavioral and functional data

claim: Silencing MBc neurons impairs odor attraction but not repulsion.
source: A behavioral study revealed that silencing MBc neurons impairs odor attraction but not repulsion (Wang et al., 2003b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2003b

claim: Odors with opposing hedonic valences are encoded by an interplay of distinct processing pathways.
source: Our data suggests that odors with opposing hedonic valences are encoded by an interplay of distinct processing pathways.
evidence: Inference from functional and behavioral data

claim: GABA release from MZ699+ iPNs directly inhibits responses of vlPr neurons to food odors.
source: The study by Liang et al. (2013) showed that GABA release from MZ699+ iPNs directly inhibits responses of vlPr neurons to food odors as mentioned above.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2013

claim: iPNs are activated mainly by attractive odors while vlPr neurons are not, likely due to the inhibitory input from iPNs.
source: This finding fits well to our observations that iPNs are activated mainly by attractive odors while vlPr neurons are not, likely due to the inhibitory input from iPNs.
evidence: Inference from functional imaging data and cited study

claim: VlPr neurons are almost solely activated by repellent odors, which do hardly activate iPNs and therefore do not induce a strong inhibition to vlPr neurons.
source: VlPr neurons are, on the other hand, almost solely activated by repellent odors, which do hardly activate iPNs and therefore do not induce a strong inhibition to vlPr neurons.
evidence: Inference from functional imaging data

claim: Repellent odors most likely activate vlPr neurons via ACh release of ePNs.
source: Repellent odors most likely activate vlPr neurons via ACh release of ePNs which is supported by immunostainings with pre- and postsynaptic markers indicating that vlPr neurons receive input in the LH, while the vlPr represents their major output region (Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Parnas et al., 2013

claim: The vlPr is supposedly also a target of visual neurons from the optic lobe.
source: The vlPr is supposedly also a target of visual neurons from the optic lobe (Tanaka et al., 2004) implying that a certain integration of different sensory modalities takes place at this central processing relay.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2004

claim: The underlying mechanism of odor attraction behavior might be an inhibition of aversive neuronal circuits from the LH to the vlPr that are mainly composed of vlPr neurons.
source: Given that iPNs are inhibitory neurons, the underlying mechanism of odor attraction behavior might therefore be an inhibition of aversive neuronal circuits from the LH to the vlPr that are mainly composed of vlPr neurons.
evidence: Speculative inference from functional and behavioral data

claim: In locusts, LH neurons receiving convergent PN input appeared to encode stimulus intensity in their net firing rates and in the phases of their spikes.
source: Notably, in locusts it has been shown that LH neurons receiving convergent PN input appeared to encode stimulus intensity in their net firing rates and in the phases of their spikes (Gupta and Stopfer, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gupta and Stopfer, 2012

claim: The representation of different pheromone types is spatially segregated in the honeybee LH.
source: Also in line with our results is a study from honeybees which shows that the representation of different pheromone types is spatially segregated in the LH (Roussel et al., 2014), indicating that odors eliciting specific behaviors are coded according to their biological values.
evidence: Supported by citation to Roussel et al., 2014

claim: The study provides functional evidence for a feature-based spatial arrangement of the LH decoding opposing hedonic valences and odor intensity.
source: In conclusion, our study provides an important step in unraveling higher olfactory processing mechanisms that are crucial for mediating innate behaviors in Drosophila. We provide functional evidence for a feature-based spatial arrangement of the LH decoding opposing hedonic valences and odor intensity.
evidence: Summary of findings from functional imaging and behavioral experiments

claim: The role of the LH as a center for integrating biological values towards innate decisions by computing conveyed information of two processing pathways is expanded.
source: The role of the LH as a center for integrating biological values towards innate decisions by computing conveyed information of two processing pathways is thus expanded.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings

claim: The olfactory system of the vinegar fly displays remarkable similarities to the mammalian system but is less complex and highly genetically tractable.
source: The olfactory system of the vinegar fly provides an excellent model system for deciphering olfactory processing mechanisms, since it displays remarkable similarities to the mammalian system but is less complex and highly genetically tractable.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Drosophila as a model system

claim: Olfactory sensory neurons with the same chemosensory receptors converge into one exclusive glomerulus in the antennal lobe.
source: This map emerges when the olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) with the same chemosensory receptors converge into one exclusive glomerulus in the antennal lobe (AL) which represents the equivalent to the mammalian olfactory bulb (Hildebrand and Shepherd, 1997; Vosshall et al., 2000; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hildebrand and Shepherd, 1997; Vosshall et al., 2000; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007

claim: The antennal lobe represents the equivalent to the mammalian olfactory bulb.
source: This map emerges when the olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) with the same chemosensory receptors converge into one exclusive glomerulus in the antennal lobe (AL) which represents the equivalent to the mammalian olfactory bulb (Hildebrand and Shepherd, 1997; Vosshall et al., 2000; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hildebrand and Shepherd, 1997; Vosshall et al., 2000; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007

claim: Glomeruli are microcircuits comprising OSNs, multiglomerular local interneurons (LNs) and uniglomerular output neurons, so-called excitatory projection neurons (ePNs).
source: Glomeruli, the functional and morphological units of the AL, are microcircuits comprising OSNs, multiglomerular local interneurons (LNs) and uniglomerular output neurons, so-called excitatory projection neurons (ePNs) (Wilson and Mainen, 2006; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007) that convey the olfactory information to higher brain centers, as the mushroom body calyx (MBc) and the lateral horn (LH) (Stocker et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wilson and Mainen, 2006; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Stocker et al., 1997

claim: ePNs convey the olfactory information to higher brain centers, as the mushroom body calyx (MBc) and the lateral horn (LH).
source: Glomeruli, the functional and morphological units of the AL, are microcircuits comprising OSNs, multiglomerular local interneurons (LNs) and uniglomerular output neurons, so-called excitatory projection neurons (ePNs) (Wilson and Mainen, 2006; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007) that convey the olfactory information to higher brain centers, as the mushroom body calyx (MBc) and the lateral horn (LH) (Stocker et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stocker et al., 1997

claim: The stringent spatial arrangement of OSNs and ePNs in the AL generates a spatial map containing characteristic combinatorial glomerular activity patterns for all odorants.
source: The stringent spatial arrangement of OSNs and ePNs in the AL generates a spatial map containing characteristic combinatorial glomerular activity patterns for all odorants (Fiala et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2003a; Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fiala et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2003a; Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005

claim: The MBc is involved in olfactory memory formation.
source: The MBc is involved in olfactory memory formation (Heisenberg, 2003) and enables a contextualization of the odor space (Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heisenberg, 2003 and Caron et al., 2013

claim: The MBc enables a contextualization of the odor space.
source: The MBc is involved in olfactory memory formation (Heisenberg, 2003) and enables a contextualization of the odor space (Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caron et al., 2013

claim: The LH is believed to be involved in innate olfactory behavior.
source: By exclusion, the LH is believed to be involved in innate olfactory behavior (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Jefferis et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Jefferis et al., 2007

claim: Excitatory PNs retain the sensory information encoded in the AL and form glomerulus-dependent, stereotypic axonal terminal fields in the LH.
source: Excitatory PNs retain the sensory information encoded in the AL and form glomerulus-dependent, stereotypic axonal terminal fields in the LH (Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2004

claim: Compartmentalization in the LH has been observed in form of a spatial segregation of ePNs innervating specific glomerular subgroups.
source: Compartmentalization in the LH has been observed in form of a spatial segregation of ePNs innervating specific glomerular subgroups (Tanaka et al., 2004), fruit and pheromone odor information processing ePNs (Jefferis et al., 2007) as well as ammonia and amine vs carbon dioxide coding ePNs (Min et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 2004; Jefferis et al., 2007; Min et al., 2013

claim: The olfactory circuit of the fly contains spatially distinct pathways to the higher brain, namely the inner, middle and outer antennocerebral tract (iACT, mACT and oACT).
source: Like many other sensory networks, the olfactory circuit of the fly contains spatially distinct pathways to the higher brain, namely the inner, middle and outer antennocerebral tract (iACT, mACT and oACT) (Stocker et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stocker et al., 1990

claim: The mACT projects from the AL to the LH exclusively and consists of inhibitory PNs (iPNs).
source: Notably, the mACT projects from the AL to the LH exclusively and consists of inhibitory PNs (iPNs), which exhibit also uniglomerular but mainly multiglomerular AL innervations (Ito et al., 1997; Jefferis et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2008; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ito et al., 1997; Jefferis et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2008; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013

claim: iPNs exhibit also uniglomerular but mainly multiglomerular AL innervations.
source: Notably, the mACT projects from the AL to the LH exclusively and consists of inhibitory PNs (iPNs), which exhibit also uniglomerular but mainly multiglomerular AL innervations (Ito et al., 1997; Jefferis et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2008; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ito et al., 1997; Jefferis et al., 2007; Lai et al., 2008; Okada et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013

claim: Both PN populations exhibit odor responses to overlapping odor ligands, but iPNs seem to be broader tuned than ePNs.
source: Although both PN populations exhibit odor responses to overlapping odor ligands, iPNs seems to be broader tuned than ePNs (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014

claim: While ePNs encode rather odor identity, iPNs have been shown to enhance innate discrimination of closely related odors.
source: Furthermore, while ePNs encode rather odor identity (Wang et al., 2003a; Wilson et al., 2004; Silbering et al., 2008), iPNs have been shown to enhance innate discrimination of closely related odors (Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2003a; Wilson et al., 2004; Silbering et al., 2008; Parnas et al., 2013

claim: PN populations process information on dual olfactory pathways and most likely accomplish different olfactory behaviors.
source: Together, these PN populations process information on dual olfactory pathways (Liang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014), as do processing mechanisms in other sensory modalities (Nassi and Callaway, 2009), and most likely accomplish different olfactory behaviors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Liang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014; Nassi and Callaway, 2009

claim: The mainly multiglomerular AL pattern of iPNs suggests that these neurons extract characteristic stimulus features from the AL code and re-integrate this information into the LH to mediate innate odorant-guided behavior.
source: The mainly multiglomerular AL pattern of iPNs suggests that these neurons extract characteristic stimulus features from the AL code and re-integrate this information into the LH to mediate innate odorant-guided behavior.
evidence: Inference from morphological observations

claim: The inhibitory input from the AL to the LH is module-specific, that is, selective for food odors and pheromones.
source: This assumption is further supported by two recent studies showing that the inhibitory input from the AL to the LH is module-specific, that is, selective for food odors and pheromones (Liang et al., 2013; Fisek and Wilson, 2014), while the connectivity in the MBc is rather probabilistic (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liang et al., 2013; Fisek and Wilson, 2014

claim: The connectivity in the MBc is rather probabilistic.
source: This assumption is further supported by two recent studies showing that the inhibitory input from the AL to the LH is module-specific, that is, selective for food odors and pheromones (Liang et al., 2013; Fisek and Wilson, 2014), while the connectivity in the MBc is rather probabilistic (Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murthy et al., 2008; Caron et al., 2013

claim: iPNs are subdivided into two morphological groups encoding positive hedonic valence or intensity information and conveying these features into separate domains in the LH.
source: We demonstrate that iPNs are subdivided into two morphological groups encoding positive hedonic valence or intensity information and conveying these features into separate domains in the LH.
evidence: Summary of findings from morphological and functional experiments

claim: Silencing iPNs severely diminished flies' attraction behavior.
source: Silencing iPNs severely diminished flies' attraction behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experimental data

claim: Functional imaging disclosed a LH region tuned to repulsive odors comprised exclusively of third-order neurons.
source: Moreover, functional imaging disclosed a LH region tuned to repulsive odors comprised exclusively of third-order neurons.
evidence: Supported by functional imaging and transection experiments
